23.0.s.en: (1) Renewal of the covenant with God

23.0.0.en: The righteous King Josiah was deeply moved by the words of the Law of God, and this led him to repentance and not to despair, despite the severity of the divine punishment. So he called all the elders of his kingdom, whether the elders of Jerusalem or the elders of the cities of Judah, as well as the priests and the prophets and all the people of Jerusalem. This shows the extent of Josiah's bearing of his responsibilities as a shepherd of the people, for he took care that the great and the small, the rulers and all the people should come to make a covenant with God; he is an example of the faithful servant. And they went up to the house of the Lord, which stood on the hills of Jerusalem. There he stood himself to read the book of the Law of God, for it is an honor for him to read the word of God, and it also shows his concern, his fear of God and his humility before Him. His reading of "all the book of the covenant" does not mean reading all five books of Moses, for that would take many hours, but the commandments and laws that were required to be carried out by all the people, which are part of the Book of Exodus and the Book of Deuteronomy, and which include all the duties of the people toward God.

23.1.1.en: His statutes: His worship with all its rites.

23.1.2.en: After Josiah read the book of the Law from a platform, that is, a place higher than the people, all the people stood, and Josiah made a covenant for himself and for all the people to obey the word of God and hold fast to His commandments and worship. They made this covenant with all their hearts, and the king took care of this so that the people would not return to the worship of idols and the doing of evil.

23.1.3.en: Josiah's reading of the Law to the people is a carrying out of the word of God that had been neglected for a long time, for God commanded that His Law be read to His people every seven years (Deut 31:10-13).

23.1.4.en: Do not be disturbed when you hear or read the stern words of God, but let this lead you to the fear of God and to being strengthened in spiritual striving, confident that God wants your salvation and will support you in your striving, whatever your weakness.

23.2.s.en: (2) The cleansing of the temple, Jerusalem and the cities of Samaria

23.2.0.en: The second order: the high priest had a group of deputies, each in charge of a group of priests. The second order means either these deputies, that is, those in authority after him, for he represents the first order, or it means one of the orders, since the priests were divided into several orders, and he chose the second order, perhaps because its priests were distinguished by godliness, zeal and rejection of evil.

23.2.1.en: The fields of Kidron: fields lying east of Jerusalem, between it and the Mount of Olives. They are beautiful places in which the worship of idols was offered, and also parks for the people. But after Josiah burned the vessels in them, they were turned into a dump where the people of Jerusalem threw all their refuse, which was burned there, and it was afterward named in this way the valley of the son of Hinnom, and the fire was always burning in it because of the abundance of the waste in it, and from it was taken the word Gehenna, whose fire is not quenched (Mt 5:22, 25:41). Josiah began by cleansing the temple, so he commanded Hilkiah the high priest, together with the priests of the second order, assisted by the keepers of the doors of the temple, to gather the vessels that they used for the worship of Baal that were inside the temple of God, because the wickedness of the former kings had reached the point that they worshiped strange gods inside the house of the Lord.

23.2.2.en: And after they gathered these vessels, they took them out to the fields of Kidron, where the worship of idols was offered, and he burned these vessels there, to defile these places which the people had anciently set apart for idols and which afterward were turned into a dump, as a declaration of the people's rejection of all pagan worship. And to confirm the rejection of the worship of idols, Josiah took the ashes of the burning and carried them to Bethel and scattered them there, to defile the place which the kings of Israel had set apart for the worship of one of the golden calves that Jeroboam made; for he cared not only for the kingdom of Judah but also for the kingdom of Israel, which had been taken captive and no longer had a king who cared for the worship of God in it. Of course, he did not burn these vessels in Jerusalem, so as not to defile the city.

23.2.3.en: Perhaps Josiah began by cleansing the temple and Jerusalem, and afterwards took care to repair the temple mentioned in the previous chapter. The cleansing, of course, took several years, and consequently Josiah would have begun the cleansing when he was about twenty years old, because he began the repair of the temple when he was twenty-six years old (ch. 22:3).

23.3.0.en: The planets (mazzaloth): a group of mansions in which the pagans believed that the gods came down and dwelt, so they called them the mansions.

23.3.1.en: Continuing the work of cleansing, Josiah drove out all the priests of the idols who offered worship to Baal, the moon, the planets and all the host of heaven, and in this he put an end to the idolatry that had spread in the days of Manasseh and Amon.

23.4.0.en: He also brought out the image of Ashtoreth, the wife of the idol-god Baal, from the temple and from all Jerusalem and threw it into the valley of Kidron, where he burned it and ground it to dust, and scattered the dust on the graves of the common people. And the grove, that is, this idol, which had been set up by the wicked King Manasseh (ch. 21:7, 2 Chr 33:15), he burned and ground and scattered its dust on the graves of the people who shared in the worship of this idol, so that this dust would become unclean in the sight of the people, because the dead were unclean and whoever touched them became unclean. By scattering it on the graves, that is, he defiled it, and in this way no one could make it again or worship it. This shows the extent of Josiah's firmness and his complete removal of evil.

23.5.0.en: Josiah also removed the houses that had been built by the house of the Lord and were set apart for sexual perversion, for some perverted men lived in them, so that men would come and commit fornication with them. And the women wove houses of cloth to be set up as tents, within which were placed images of the grove, and sexual perversion was practiced in these tents as well. This shows the extent of the people's degradation in their worship of idols, so Josiah cleansed the temple and what is around it of all these evils. It also shows how the house of the Lord had been turned into a house for the worship of idols in the days of the former wicked kings, and now Josiah restores it to be for the worship of God alone, with worship practiced within it in complete purity and cleanness.

23.6.0.en: Geba: a city in Benjamin on the northern edge of Judah.

23.6.1.en: Beersheba: the capital of the Negev, the farthest south of Judah.

23.6.2.en: Josiah gathered the priests of the Lord from all the land, from the farthest north to the farthest south of the kingdom of Judah, so that worship would be only in the temple of God in Jerusalem and no worship of God would be offered on the high places, as the kings had permitted, not only the wicked among them but also the righteous, and many of his descendants. He also defiled all the places of worship that had been set up for the Lord, or for the idols, on the hills, by burning the bones of the dead on them or by any means, so that no one would approach them afterward for worship. This included all the high places scattered throughout the kingdom of Judah, from one end to the other. Likewise the people had been accustomed to offer worship at the gates of the city of Jerusalem, where towers were built, which made them high places, so he removed all the images of the idols and the altars set up at the gates, such as the altar set up at the gate of Jerusalem, on the left, which was before the house of Joshua the governor of the city.

23.7.0.en: As for the priests who continued to offer sacrifices to the Lord on the high places in the days of Manasseh, Josiah did not allow them to use the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem, although he permitted them to eat unleavened bread among their brethren the priests; that is, they did not continue in their priestly work as a punishment for them, because they offered worship in a place other than the house of the Lord, and this is against the Law. But at the same time he took care of their food, so they ate like the rest of their brethren, as was done with the priests who had bodily defects (Lev 21:21-23), so they ate of the bread of the offerings presented in the house of the Lord, which the priests had a right to eat, which is the unleavened bread (Lev 6:16-18).

23.7.1.en: In your firmness with others, if you are compelled to punish someone, to establish justice and truth, do not forget the needs of the one punished, for he is a human being; that is, be merciful also in your punishment, that you may lead everyone to life with God.

23.8.0.en: The valley of the children of Hinnom: it lies southeast of Jerusalem, between the Horse Gate and the well of Job, and the children of Hinnom is the name of a Canaanite tribe.

23.8.1.en: Tophet: a place in the valley of the children of Hinnom for burning human bodies, where human sacrifices were offered to the god Molech.

23.8.2.en: Molech: the god of the children of Ammon. They made for him a hollow bronze statue of a seated man with his hands stretched out before him, and lit a fire under it until the bronze became red with heat, then they passed the children between his hands to hallow them and consecrate them to this god, and their bodies were scorched by the extremely hot bronze. They also placed some children on his hands as a sacrifice, and they were burned by the intense heat, and they beat drums loudly so that they would not hear the cries of the children as they died. The word Tophet means a drum, so they called the place Tophet.

23.8.3.en: One of the most famous places of idol worship near Jerusalem was the area of Tophet, which was set apart for the worship of the god Molech and lies in the valley of the children of Hinnom. King Josiah took care to defile this area, to stop the atrocities that took place there, the passing of children through the fire or offering them as sacrifices to this pagan god.

23.9.0.en: The worshipers of the sun set apart chariots drawn by horses, with which they went out before the sun, and the horses, because of their speed, represented the sun, which moves in the sky. The wicked kings before Josiah used to give horses to those who worshiped the sun. So Josiah destroyed the horses that were used in the worship of the sun, so that the people would not think them holy. He also burned the chariots of the sun, to remove any trace of sun worship, and of course he gave no more horses after that to these pagan worships. These horses were near the chamber of Nathan-melech, which was inside the house of the Lord, in one of the colonnades. Nathan-melech was one of the king's eunuchs and perhaps was the one in charge of these horses.

23.10.0.en: Ahaz had built an upper chamber on top of one of the buildings of the temple of the Lord, and because he was wicked and neglected worship in the house of the Lord, he may have built this upper room for his private needs, or for the worship of idols. But Manasseh and Amon, the wicked kings of Judah, built altars on it for the worship of the host of heaven; that is, they worshiped idols above the temple of the Lord. King Manasseh also set up altars for the idols in the two courts of the house of the Lord, that is, the inner court for the priests and the outer court for the people. We understand from this how widespread the worship of idols was, not only in Jerusalem, the holy city, but also inside the house of the Lord, in the days of the wicked kings. All this the righteous Josiah removed and broke until it became dust, and he supervised the work himself, then hurried, carrying this dust, and scattered it in the valley of Kidron, where idol worship had been practiced, and defiled it. All this shows Josiah's zeal, for he does the work himself and hurries to get rid of the traces of pagan worship in the temple and to defile the place of idol worship in the valley of Kidron.

23.11.0.en: The mount of corruption: the southern part of the Mount of Olives, and the Mount of Olives lies east of Jerusalem and was afterward called by this name because of the abundance of idol worship on it.

23.11.1.en: The Zidonians: the inhabitants of Sidon, which is on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea.

23.11.2.en: The Moabites: they lived east of the river Jordan and the Dead Sea.

23.11.3.en: The children of Ammon: they lived east of the river Jordan.

23.11.4.en: Solomon had set up on the hills south of the Mount of Olives altars for the worship of famous pagan gods, such as Ashtoreth, the unclean goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh, the defiled god of the Moabites, and Molech, the god of the children of Ammon, whose worship God hates. All these altars and the idols before them and the groves, that is, the pillars set up for the pagan gods, the righteous Josiah broke in pieces, and he was not content with removing them, but also defiled their place by putting the bones of the dead on them, and whoever touched these bones became unclean (Lev 21:1), and in this way no one could worship idols in these places again. Thus the places of worship of the pagan gods, who symbolize fertility and life, were turned into places for the bones of the dead; that is, they became a symbol of death and not of life, and by this he meant to remove the idea of idol worship from the minds of the people, that they might hate it.

23.11.5.en: When you drive out any strange thought that defiles your mind, take care also to repeat the Psalms and prayers, so as to remove every trace of evil from your thinking and replace it with the thoughts of God, remembering also the danger of these thoughts, which lead to judgment and destruction, so that you hasten to drive them out.

23.12.0.en: Josiah's heart was inflamed with the love of God, so he wanted to cleanse the whole world of the worship of idols. He was not content with cleansing the kingdom of Judah over which he reigned, but his concern extended to the kingdom of Israel, which had fallen into captivity. As a result of the weakness of the Assyrian empire, which had dominated the whole world and the kingdom of Israel, he moved by the power of God to remove the worship of idols from Bethel, which Jeroboam the son of Nebat had established, who split the kingdom of Israel. That is, Josiah wanted to remove the beginning and the roots of the worship of idols from Israel, so he went to Bethel, the most important place of idol worship, and removed from the high places there the altar and the grove and all the buildings connected with idol worship. He broke them down and burned the wood in them, and crushed everything until it became dust, and scattered it; that is, he protected the land from every trace of pagan worship.

23.13.0.en: While Josiah was destroying idol worship in Bethel, he learned of the existence of tombs near the place, so he sent and brought out the bones of the dead and burned them on the altar to defile it, so that no one would try to offer idol worship again in this place. In this he fulfilled the word of God that a prophet had spoken about Jeroboam about three hundred years before, that a king named Josiah would come and remove the idol worship that Jeroboam had made in Bethel (1 Kgs 13:2).

23.14.0.en: Title: a stone or pillar set up to declare the presence of a grave in this place, and sometimes used as a mark on the road.

23.14.1.en: Out of Samaria: not from the city of Samaria, but from one of its cities; he was from Bethel, which belonged to Samaria.

23.14.2.en: The king noticed a monument in the place and asked, Whose is it? The men of the city answered him that it was the grave of the man of God who came from Judah and foretold all that he had done at Bethel.

23.14.3.en: And Josiah commanded that the bones of the prophet not be moved, nor the bones of the other prophet, who was from one of the cities of Samaria, that is, from Bethel, who was buried with him (1 Kgs 13:11), in honor of the prophet who came from Judah, who prophesied the removal of idol worship.

23.15.0.en: Josiah was not content with removing idol worship from Bethel, but his cleansing extended also to the various cities of Samaria. He removed from their high places the worship of idols, that is, the altars, groves and buildings set up for it, and burned the bones of the dead on them to defile them so that they would not be used again for worship, and scattered their ashes, as he did at Bethel. We notice from this his continued concern to cleanse of idol worship every place his hand could reach, so that the kingdom of Judah, and also the kingdom of Israel, which had been taken captive, would be clean of pagan worship.

23.16.0.en: Josiah commanded that all the priests of the high places in Samaria be killed upon their pagan altars, and he burned the bones of the dead on them, then returned to Jerusalem.

23.16.1.en: Josiah was compelled to slay the priests of the idols during the cleansing from this worship, because God had been longsuffering with them until they led astray many of the simple people, so Josiah had to be firm and stop the source of evil, who were these priests.

23.16.2.en: And although the people of the kingdom of Israel had walked for many long years in the worship of idols, they accepted what Josiah did, as they accepted what the prophet Elijah did of old when he slew the prophets of Baal (1 Kgs 18:40), because the people know in their depths that God alone is the true God and that all these worships, however many years they may have continued, are vain.

23.16.3.en: Do not be afraid to proclaim the voice of God with power, however prevalent evil may be, to awaken the conscience of those who are far away, and God will support you; only take care to pray well before you speak, so that the words may be from God and not out of pride or personal motive. You are responsible to speak, to rescue the lost and those far away.

23.17.s.en: (3) The Passover and the removal of sorcery

23.17.0.en: After Josiah's concern for cleansing Jerusalem, Judea and the cities of Samaria, he began the positive side of the reforms by calling for the keeping of the feast of the Passover, which the Law prescribed in the book of the covenant that they had found in the temple. He called all the people of Jerusalem and Judea and also the people of the kingdom of Israel, for Josiah was a preacher of God everywhere (2 Chr 35:18).

23.18.0.en: The celebration of the Passover that Josiah kept was a magnificent celebration, whose splendor was not equaled by any of the Passover celebrations that the children of Israel held since the days of Samuel, that is, for more than five centuries; that is, Josiah's Passover surpassed in splendor the Passover that Hezekiah kept, and it was said that none like it had been kept since the days of Solomon. The excellence of Josiah's Passover lay in his concern to carry out the Law with all exactness, as God had declared to Moses, and also in his giving from his own wealth very many lambs, numbered in thousands, which encouraged the princes to give lambs also (2 Chr 35:1-19). When this Passover was kept in Jerusalem, King Josiah was twenty-six years old. From this we understand that he began the positive reforms, from the repair of the temple and the Passover, in the eighteenth year of his reign, whereas the cleansing operations were during the preceding years.

23.18.1.en: May you take care that your worship of God is with all your heart, and also care for His holy feasts and the building of His churches, giving generously, for this shows your love for Him and the extent of your attachment to Him, and stirs your spiritual feelings.

23.19.0.en: The teraphim: small images of the pagan gods placed in the house for people to worship, in addition to the large images set up in the temples.

23.19.1.en: Along with his positive reforms, Josiah continued the work of cleansing, not only of the idols set up in the pagan temples but also of the teraphim found in the homes, for he was firm with the people in making them bring the teraphim out of their houses so that he might destroy them. He also did away with the sorcerers and diviners and all who deal with demons to know the future, or any demonic works. In sum, he took care to cleanse Jerusalem and Judea of all causes of evil that violate the Law. And in this he fulfilled the word of God that he found in the book of the Law that was found in the temple.

23.20.s.en: (4) The excellence of the righteous Josiah, then his death

23.20.0.en: God declares clearly here the distinction of Josiah above all the former and later kings of Judah. Though some kings were distinguished, such as Hezekiah and Asa, they come after him in rank, because he took care with all his heart to carry out the Law of God. He was the king who took most care to cleanse his country of the worship of idols and of all the altars set up on the high places. And although he knew of God's punishment that would come upon the kingdom of Judah after the end of his life, he did not grow slack, but on the contrary moved with unusual energy to glorify the name of God in Judah and Israel, after His name had been insulted for long years before. He is a symbol of hope, righteousness and perseverance in spiritual striving, in addition to firmness and strength in declaring the truth, so that he deserves to be called the second of the kings after David in spiritual rank, for he resembled his forefather David in that he arose in the midst of a wicked generation far from God and clearly proclaimed the name of God.

23.21.0.en: Despite the greatness of the reforms that Josiah made, God did not turn back from His decision to punish the kingdom of Judah, because the people, who had gone astray in the days of Manasseh and his son Amon and responded to Josiah, responded superficially and not from the whole heart, as is proved by the fact that the kings who came after Josiah, who were his sons, walked in evil and returned to the worship of idols, so they deserved divine punishment. This shows two things:

23.21.1.en: 1- The extent to which evil had spread and ruled over the hearts of the people of God.

23.21.2.en: 2- The greatness of Josiah, who appeared in a wicked generation, for the kings before him and after him were wicked.

23.22.0.en: Because of the evils of the people of God, God insisted on His decision to abandon the kingdom of Judah, as He had abandoned the kingdom of Israel, and to leave His temple to be torn down and burned in the destruction of Jerusalem and Judea. All this was because of the superficiality of His people's worship and the attachment of their hearts to idols.

23.22.1.en: Beware of superficial worship, practicing everything formally, without understanding or feeling, and being content with the appearance without the substance, for this does not please God but provokes Him. Ask God's help to repent of your sins and try to understand every act of worship you offer Him, and He will grant you, not only forgiveness, but also that you feel Him and delight in being with Him.

23.23.0.en: The rest of the works that Josiah did are recorded in the "Book of the Chronicles of the kings of Judah."

23.24.0.en: In the thirty-first year of the reign of Josiah, the king of Egypt, Pharaoh Necho, attacked the king of Assyria, who had become weak at this time, and Pharaoh seized the opportunity to take possession of the territories belonging to him in Syria. Josiah felt fear for his country, lest Pharaoh seize it, so he went out to fight him and did not consult God, and Pharaoh tried to keep him out of the war, because he wanted to fight the king of Assyria, but Josiah erred and attacked Pharaoh, and Pharaoh killed him at the city of Megiddo, inflicting on him a mortal wound. We notice that Solomon is a type of Christ in the building of the temple, as Christ founded the Church. Hezekiah is also a type of Christ in the extension of his life by fifteen years after he had been condemned to death by his illness, and Christ after His death had His life extended forever. As for Josiah, he is a type of Christ in his death outside Jerusalem at the hands of his enemies at Megiddo, as Christ was crucified outside Jerusalem at Golgotha.

23.25.0.en: The soldiers under Josiah carried their king with his mortal wound until they reached Jerusalem, and he died there (2 Chr 35:24) and they buried him, then his son Jehoahaz reigned after him. For the original word translated in the previous verse as "killed him" means, in its origin, that he was wounded with a mortal wound and did not die at once.

23.26.s.en: (5) Jehoahaz reigns over Judah and is taken captive

23.26.0.en: Libnah: it lies thirty-two kilometers from Jerusalem and is thirteen kilometers from Lachish to the northeast, southwest of Jerusalem.

23.26.1.en: Jehoahaz was not the firstborn, who should have reigned in place of his father, but was fourth in order among his brothers. The sons of Josiah are: the firstborn Johanan, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum, who is also called Jehoahaz. The people thought he was the best of his brothers, so they made him king after his father Josiah.

23.26.2.en: Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when the people anointed him king, and his reign lasted only three months. His mother's name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of the town of Libnah, and he is, of course, not the prophet Jeremiah, who was from Anathoth, not Libnah.

23.26.3.en: These three months in which Jehoahaz reigned are the period after the death of his father in the war, when Pharaoh of Egypt, who was called Necho, killed him; this Pharaoh went on his way with his armies to Carchemish, which lies west of the river Euphrates, then returned, leaving his armies at Carchemish, and to show his authority over the kingdom of Judah, he deposed Jehoahaz, took him captive and brought him to Egypt. After that he went to Carchemish and was defeated before Nebuchadnezzar, and the king of Babylon took possession of the region of the Levant as far as Egypt.

23.27.0.en: Neither the Book of Kings nor the Book of Chronicles mentions the evils of Jehoahaz, but the writer of the Book of Kings was content to mention the summary, which is that he did evil in the sight of the Lord, following in this the footsteps of his forefathers, that is, Manasseh and Amon.

23.27.1.en: But we can deduce from (Jer 23:10-17 and Ezek 19:1-5) that he committed many evil deeds. Ezekiel describes him in (Ezek 19:1-5) as one who "learned to catch the prey; it devoured men." He devoured his people, and came to work for himself and not for the kingdom.

23.27.2.en: And we wonder how he was able in only three months to show his evil, and this shows that he learned nothing from his righteous father and seized the opportunity of his reign to hasten to evil. This also shows that the people's choice of him was not on the basis of righteousness and goodness, but by human standards, because the people had not repented truly in the days of Josiah. It seems that Josiah was firm in his cleansing of evil, but he was not given great opportunity to teach the people, so their repentance was weak.

23.27.3.en: May we not love ourselves, but be like our beloved Shepherd and Redeemer, who did not seek His own but ours, who said, "The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister." "He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life shall find it."

23.28.0.en: Riblah: a city in the land of Hamath, in the present state of Syria, lying north of the Sea of Galilee. A talent of silver: it has several weights, ranging between 20 and 40 kg.

23.28.1.en: A talent of gold: equal to 17.4 kg.

23.28.2.en: Pharaoh Necho returned to Riblah, which is north of the kingdom of Judah, and summoned Jehoahaz and arrested him and sent him to Egypt as a prisoner, and he ordered an enormous tribute upon Judah, amounting to a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. The people of the kingdom paid this sum, whereas in the days of Hezekiah the gold and silver were paid from the treasuries of the house of the Lord and the house of the king and the gold stripped from the house of the Lord, and it did not burden the people, although the sum paid in the days of Hezekiah was far greater than that required in the days of Jehoahaz and his brother Jehoiakim, who reigned after him (ch. 18:

23.29.0.en: Jehoiakim: its meaning is "Jehovah will raise up," whereas Eliakim means "God will raise up." Pharaoh changed his name as a kind of imposition of authority, but, by God's arrangement, the men of Judah suggested this name to him, and it is a name with a beautiful spiritual meaning, because Jehovah is the God of Israel and not just any god, perhaps in order to benefit the king of Judah; but sadly he did not learn from his new name and departed from God.

23.29.1.en: Necho made Eliakim, the elder brother of Jehoahaz, king in his place and changed his name from Eliakim to Jehoiakim. Jehoahaz came to Egypt and died there, in fulfillment of the prophecy of Jeremiah, who said of him: "Thus saith the Lord touching Shallum the son of Josiah (Shallum is the original name of Jehoahaz, before his name was changed when he ascended the throne), which went forth out of this place; he shall not return thither any more: but he shall die in the place whither they have led him captive, and shall see this land no more" (Jer 22:10-12). This is the first time a brother, and not a son, reigned on the throne of the kingdom of Judah. Because of the evil of Jehoahaz, Pharaoh of Egypt deposed him and took him captive, imposed a tribute on the land of Judah and made his brother king in his place. But when the people believed in the days of Moses and sought God, He smote Pharaoh and his people and brought them out with an uplifted arm; so when we are with God, He protects us and gives us victory over our enemies the demons, but when we walk in evil, He forsakes us, and we are humbled.

23.29.2.en: Hold fast to the commandments of God and to His worship, and He will protect you and give you victory in all your wars with the demons, and you will live in peace however much troubles surround you.

23.30.1.en: Jehoiakim undertook to pay the tribute of silver and gold to Pharaoh, but he imposed taxes on the people of the land, according to what they possessed, so as to be able to pay it.

23.31.0.en: Rumah: it is Khirbet Rumah, ten kilometers north of Nazareth.

23.31.1.en: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign over Judah in the capital Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zebudah the daughter of Pedaiah of the town of "Rumah."

23.32.0.en: Sadly, Jehoiakim walked in evil like his brother Jehoahaz and learned nothing from the righteousness of his father. The Book of the prophet Jeremiah gives us details of this king's evils: he was selfish, seizing the rights of others, far from God (Jer 26:21-24).

23.32.1.en: May you learn from the righteousness and virtues of those around you, and also take warning from the evils of others, because all these are messages sent to you. Jehoiakim did not learn from the righteousness of Josiah nor from the evils of his brother Jehoahaz, who was taken captive to Egypt.

23.32.2.en: Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah, the last kings of Judah
